blocks.text: The first law of thermodynamics tells us that heat energy can be converted into an equivalent amount of work, but it is silent about the conditions under which this conversion takes place. The second law is concerned with the circumstances in which heat can be converted into work and the direction of flow of heat.

Before the formal statement, consider the factual operation of an engine. The engine or the system (Fig. 6.8) absorbs a quantity of heat Q1 from the heat source at temperature T1; it does work W and expels heat Q2 to a low-temperature reservoir at temperature T2. As the working substance goes through a cyclic process in which it eventually returns to its initial state, the change in internal energy is zero; hence from the first law the net work done equals the net heat absorbed: W = Q1 - Q2. In practice the petrol engine of a motor car extracts heat from the burning fuel, converts a fraction of this energy to mechanical energy or work and expels the rest to the atmosphere; it has been observed that petrol engines convert roughly 25% and diesel engines 35 to 40% of the available heat energy into work.

blocks.title: Second law (Lord Kelvin's statement)
blocks.text: The second law is a formal statement based on these observations and can be stated in a number of ways. According to Lord Kelvin's statement, based on the working of a heat engine: it is impossible to devise a process which may convert heat, extracted from a single reservoir, entirely into work without leaving any change in the working system.

This means that a single heat reservoir, no matter how much energy it contains, cannot be made to perform any work. This is true for the oceans and our atmosphere, which contain a large amount of heat energy but cannot be converted into useful mechanical work. As a consequence of the second law, two bodies at different temperatures are essential for the conversion of heat into work: for the working of a heat engine there must be a source of heat at a high temperature and a sink at low temperature to which heat may be expelled. The reason for our inability to utilise the heat contents of the oceans and atmosphere is that there is no reservoir at a temperature lower than any one of the two. The process pictured in the Tidbits box, heat from a source at a single temperature converted entirely into work, is impossible.

blocks.caption: Heat engine, second law, Carnot cycle, refrigerator and entropy (original diagram after Figures 6.8 to 6.10 and topics 6.6 to 6.11).
blocks.long_description: A heat engine takes heat from a hot reservoir, turns part of it into work and rejects the rest to a cold reservoir, so over a cycle the work equals the difference of the two heats; Kelvin's statement of the second law says no device can turn heat from a single reservoir wholly into work, which is why a source and a sink are both needed. Carnot's ideal engine runs a reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats, and its efficiency, one minus the ratio of the cold to the hot absolute temperature, is the greatest any engine between those temperatures can have, reaching unity only for a sink at absolute zero. A refrigerator is the engine run backwards, pumping heat from a cold space to warmer surroundings by means of work, with a coefficient of performance equal to the heat removed divided by the work. Entropy change is the heat exchanged divided by the absolute temperature; natural heat flow from hot to cold raises the total entropy, so the entropy of the universe always increases, energy becomes less available for work, and melting ice gains entropy as its molecules grow more disordered.

blocks.prompt: State the second law in two different forms, and say whether a cyclic reversible engine can absorb heat at one temperature and turn it completely into work (short questions 6.3, 6.9).
blocks.explanation: Kelvin: no process can convert heat extracted from a single reservoir entirely into work without leaving a change in the working system. Clausius: heat cannot of itself flow from a colder to a hotter body. Entropy form: a natural process goes in the direction that raises the entropy of the system plus its surroundings. No: a cyclic engine must reject some heat to a colder sink, otherwise it would violate Kelvin's statement; a source alone cannot run it.

items: Engine: absorbs Q1 at T1, does W, rejects Q2 at T2; W = Q1 - Q2 (petrol about 25%, diesel 35 to 40%). Kelvin: heat from a single reservoir cannot be wholly converted into work; a source and a sink at different temperatures are essential, so the oceans and atmosphere cannot drive an engine.
